claims.claim: Hartlage says Curse of Strahd gives pages of room description to notable NPCs' homes and calls Chris Perkins's details creepy and moody while judging most of those rooms unreachable in play.
claims.quote: The homes of notable NPCs get pages of room descriptions.
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage reports that Curse of Strahd carries boxed text for every location while its successor Storm King's Thunder omits almost all read-aloud text.
Justin Alexander's judgment on the state of the form is that published adventures' location keys are almost all bad.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: the location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible

claims.claim: Alexander says a standardised section format pushes writers to fill every heading, so a Tactics section gets paragraphs even when the orcs have only swords.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: it tends to encourage writers to “fill the format”

claims.claim: Alexander makes the order of a location description depend on the scene rather than a fixed template, contrasting a visible ogre with a hidden goblin.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: A room with an ogre standing in the middle of it

claims.claim: Alexander dates the arrival of boxed text to Lost Tamoachan and says the prewritten descriptions appeared between quotation marks before TSR boxed them in the 1980 reissue.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: the text was not yet boxed, instead appearing between quotation marks

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch diagnoses Lost Mine of Phandelver's generic feel as a failure of modifiers rather than of nouns and verbs.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of Lost Mine of Phandelver, tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: the adjectives and adverbs were not used very well

claims.claim: Lynch shows the cure as a single added modifier before a role noun and lists six alternatives that would each conjure a different woman.
claims.quote: the prim farmers wife tells you

claims.claim: Lynch's complaint about the Phandalin section is that the town's language is thin outside its core locations.
claims.quote: quite light on descriptive and evocative language

claims.claim: Lynch asks for a web of stated relationships among a town's named residents so the place exists apart from the party.
claims.quote: a web of personal relationships between the various people living in town

claims.claim: Lynch calls the one-sentence-per-NPC summary of who is in town, where they are and what they want invaluable and asks for more adventures to carry one.
claims.quote: That’s done in just a sentence or so each.

claims.claim: Lynch says a monster entry should tell the DM what the characters sense, and offers a smell and a coat as the missing kind of detail.
claims.quote: what the PC’s EXPERIENCE when they meet them

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch calls much of Curse of Strahd's read-aloud laughable and quotes single-sentence examples from it, among them one that names nothing at all.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of Curse of Strahd, tenfootpole.org, quoting Curse of Strahd
claims.quote: You find something on the ground.

claims.claim: Lynch's charge against Curse of Strahd's prose is a fixed inflation ratio, three sentences doing one sentence's work.
claims.quote: Three sentences are used when one will do.

claims.claim: Lynch credits Curse of Strahd with villages whose residents each have something going on, and says events attached to locations are what make the places feel alive.
claims.quote: The villagers and places, in particular, seem more alive
